description: We are ucalgary students excited about aerospace!
summary:
Planetary Twin: Mars Drill-Site Analog Finder

Before a drill goes to Mars, it should be tested somewhere on Earth where the ground behaves the same way. Planetary Twin finds those places. Click any spot on Mars and pick a depth, from the surface down past 3 m. The app ranks 8,019 bare-ground Earth sites on temperature, ice, rock type, hardness and terrain, and explains every match: what it matched on and what differs. Reverse mode asks the opposite question: where on Mars is like this place on Earth?

The Mars side uses NASA data: MOLA terrain, TES thermal inertia, Odyssey neutron hydrogen, the USGS geologic map and the Mars Climate Database. The Earth side uses ESA CCI Permafrost, ERA5-Land, MODIS, SoilGrids and GLiM. Where Earth data stops, machine learning fills the gap:

a gradient-boosted ground-ice classifier, tested on regions it never saw;
a physics-informed PyTorch network that predicts ground temperature down to 10 m. It is 2.5–3× closer than a simple heat model, and its physics term cuts impossible depth profiles from 32% to 8%.
A 5-model ensemble flags places it has never seen anything like, so the app knows when it doesn't know. On 12 published Mars–Earth analog pairs, the known Earth site lands in the top 10 about 11× more often than chance.
details:
Planetary Twin finds the place on Earth whose ground behaves like a chosen spot on Mars, and the reverse. Mars drills are tested on Earth first, at sites whose ground resembles the target, but those sites are usually picked from experience and a few well-known locations. We turn that choice into a search.

What it does: Click anywhere on a 3D Mars globe, or pick a landing site such as Jezero, Gale or Phoenix, and choose a drilling depth: 0–10 cm, 10 cm–1 m, 1–3 m or deeper than 3 m. The app ranks every bare-ground cell on Earth by how closely its temperature, frozen season, ground ice, ground type, hardness, rock, slope, roughness and dryness match the Mars site at that depth. Each result shows a match %, a confidence level, what matched and what differed, satellite views of both planets, a ground profile through all four depths, and past drill campaigns there. Strong matches outside known analog regions are flagged as new candidate test sites. A reverse mode scores all 12,600 Mars cells for any Earth place or city. Other features: a drill-difficulty map, a printable mission brief, live weight sliders and shareable links.

How it works: We compute the same features on both planets. A 1-D heat-conduction model uses MGS TES thermal inertia and Mars Climate Database temperatures to estimate underground temperatures. Mars Odyssey neutron data gives ice, MOLA gives terrain and the USGS Geologic Map of Mars gives rock. Earth layers come from ERA5-Land, MODIS, ESA CCI Permafrost, SoilGrids, GLiM, NASA ORNL regolith thickness, Copernicus DEM and WorldCover. Matching uses a weighted Gower distance, which handles mixed data and missing values.

Machine learning, tested honestly: A ground-ice classifier (gradient boosting and PyTorch) fills gaps in the permafrost map. It reaches 0.97 balanced accuracy on held-out regions, against 0.54 for a latitude-only baseline. A physics-informed PyTorch network predicts ground temperature to 10 m and is about 2.8× more accurate than the heat model. The weights learned from 12 literature analog pairs did not beat our hand-tuned weights, and we say so. The matcher puts the known analog in its top 10 for 25% of pairs, against 2% by chance.

Impact: Mission and instrument teams get a fast, explainable way to choose test sites for a specific landing site and depth, including sites that are cheaper or closer to reach than Antarctica.

Tools: Python (pandas, xarray, rasterio, scikit-learn, PyTorch), Google Earth Engine, NASA Earthdata, pytest with GitHub Actions, and a JavaScript + Leaflet front end on GitHub Pages. It has no server and needs no API key.

Factors we considered: Every value is tagged as measured, modelled or predicted. Confidence drops with depth, every accuracy figure is shown next to a baseline, and the limitations are stated in the app. Results are leads for choosing field-test sites, not drilling-safety certification.
